title: DNA Analysis Reveals Seychelles' Lost Crocodiles Were Saltwater Giants
summary: For centuries, the Seychelles archipelago held a secret: what kind of crocodiles once basked on its shores? Early explorers reported them, but by the early 1800s, they were gone—exterminated by settlers. Now, a genetic analysis published by researchers from Germany and the Seychelles has finally identified these vanished reptiles. They were saltwater crocodiles (Crocodylus porosus), the world's largest living reptile and a master of ocean travel. The study, led by Stefanie Agne of the University of Potsdam and Frank Glaw of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History, compared mitochondrial DNA from historical museum specimens with modern saltwater crocodiles. The results confirmed that the Seychelles population was not a separate species but the westernmost outpost of Crocodylus porosus. "The founders of the Seychelles population must have drifted at least 3,000 kilometers across the Indian Ocean," said Glaw, senior author. Saltwater crocodiles possess specialized salt glands that allow them to excrete excess salt, enabling survival in seawater for extended periods. This adaptation likely allowed them to disperse across vast stretches of ocean, riding currents over generations. Today, the species ranges from India to northern Australia, but before the Seychelles population was wiped out, its distribution spanned over 12,000 kilometers—from Vanuatu in the Pacific to the Seychelles in the Indian Ocean. The genetic patterns suggest that saltwater crocodile populations remained connected over long periods, pointing to their high mobility. This discovery not only solves a historical puzzle but also highlights the impact of human settlement on island ecosystems. Within about 50 years of permanent colonization, the crocodiles were completely eliminated. The research underscores the value of museum collections in unlocking evolutionary histories. By extracting DNA from centuries-old specimens, scientists can reconstruct lost populations and understand how species adapted to changing environments. It's a reminder that even the most formidable predators can vanish quickly when humans arrive, and that the ocean, far from being a barrier, can be a highway for life.
why_it_matters: This finding illustrates how easily even powerful animals can be driven to local extinction when humans arrive, and it underscores the hidden value of museum collections in piecing together lost biological histories that can inform modern conservation.

background_read: The Seychelles (an island nation in the Indian Ocean, northeast of Madagascar) were uninhabited until the late 18th century, when French settlers arrived, followed by the British.
Saltwater crocodiles (Crocodylus porosus) are the largest living reptiles and are known to swim across open ocean; modern individuals have been spotted hundreds of kilometers from land.
Mitochondrial DNA (genetic code passed only through the mother) is often used to trace family trees and population movements because it changes relatively slowly over time.
Museum specimens (preserved animal skins, bones, and other remains stored in research collections) can hold centuries-old DNA, giving scientists a window into the past without needing living animals.
The rapid extinction of the Seychelles crocodiles—within about 50 years of colonization—mirrors the fate of other island species worldwide once humans and invasive animals arrived.

perspectives.description: After two centuries of uncertainty, genetic evidence finally answers a long-standing question about the Seychelles' lost crocodiles, demonstrating the power of modern molecular tools to solve historical mysteries. The global range of the species becomes clearer, enriching our understanding of animal dispersal.

The story is a stark reminder of the devastation caused by European colonization on island ecosystems. Within a single human lifetime, a population that had survived for millennia was completely erased, a loss that can never be reversed.

The research highlights how museum specimens—often collected decades or centuries ago—can hold invaluable genetic information that modern scientists can unlock. This pattern of using old DNA to reconstruct extinct populations is becoming increasingly common in evolutionary biology.

The same techniques could be applied to other extinct island populations, guiding reintroduction efforts or helping assess the genetic health of surviving relatives. The study also prompts reflection on how to protect remaining large predators that still roam the world's oceans.
